categories.name: Comb Honey
categories.title: Comb Honey
categories.intro: Single-flower and seasonal honeys, packed with a piece of real honeycomb in every box. Each one tastes of the flowers the bees visited: drumstick blossoms, sunflower fields, mustard in winter bloom, coriander, or a whole season of wildflowers.

categories.name: Blossom Honey
categories.title: Blossom Honey
categories.intro: Single-flower honeys, each from one kind of bloom: coffee flowers in the shade of forest trees, the lilac karanji tree, litchi orchards in spring and fields of flowering tulasi. Every jar tastes of its flower.

categories.name: Wild & Rare
categories.title: Wild & Rare
categories.intro: Honey from bees nobody keeps and flowers nobody plants: the stingless dammar bee that stores honey in tiny resin pots, the dwarf honey bee that hangs a single comb from a wild branch, and the Neela Kurinji hills of the Western Ghats. Harvests are small and seasonal.

categories.name: From the Hive

products.name: Murungai Honey
products.tagline: Gathered from the blossoms of the drumstick tree.

gallery.caption: Beezy moringa honey comb, as packed

products.about: Murungai honey is gathered by bees from the small cream-white flowers of the drumstick tree, found in almost every Tamil home garden. It is amber in colour, with a mild sweetness and a light herbal note. Moringa blooms only in certain seasons, so this single-flower honey comes in limited batches, with a piece of raw honeycomb in every box.
love: Single-flower honey from moringa blossoms
Mild taste the whole family enjoys
A natural source of quick energy
Real honeycomb in the box: raw and edible
products.use: Stir a spoonful into warm water in the morning, drizzle over dosa or chapati, or add to herbal kashayam once it has cooled a little.
products.store: Store at room temperature with the lid closed. Always use a dry spoon.

products.about: Forest honey comes from wild hives that bees build high in trees and on rock faces deep inside the forest, most often by the giant rock bee. The nectar comes from countless wild trees and flowers that no farm can grow. The result is a dark, thick honey with a bold, rich flavour and a slightly woody finish, harvested by hand in small batches.

It crystallises quickly and naturally, often within a few weeks, turning soft and creamy. That is a sign of real, unprocessed honey, not spoilage.

products.about: Native honey comes from the Indian honey bee, which has lived alongside our farms and villages for generations and nests in hollows and burrows. Native bees forage on local flowers close to the hive, so the honey carries the true taste of the land around it. It is usually lighter in body, with a fresh sweetness and a gentle tang.

products.about: Forest coffee honey comes from the white blossoms of coffee plants growing in the shade of tall forest trees. The coffee bushes flower for only a few days after the first rains, filling the grove with a jasmine-like scent, and the bees work the flowers while they last. The honey is light amber to amber, with caramel and soft fruity notes. It does not taste of coffee; it tastes of the flowers.

products.about: Litchi honey is made when bees visit the small, creamy flowers of litchi trees, a few months before the fruit ripens. The orchards bloom for a short season, so the harvest is quick and seasonal. It is light amber, with a floral, gently fruity taste and an aroma that recalls the litchi blossom itself. Like many light honeys, it can set into a soft cream over time, which is natural.

products.name: Dammar Honey
products.tagline: Tiny bees, rare honey, a tangy taste.

gallery.caption: Resin honey pots of the stingless bee
Stingless bee boxes among the coconut palms
Stingless bees at their resin entrance tube

products.about: Dammar honey is made by tiny stingless bees that store their honey in small pots of wax and plant resin instead of combs. A single colony gives only a few hundred grams a year, which makes it one of the rarest honeys in India. It is thin and runny, with a distinct sweet-sour taste and a resin aroma that comes from the hive itself.
love: From stingless dammar bees
Very small harvests: a truly rare honey
Distinct sweet-sour taste and resin aroma
Prized in traditional home remedies
products.use: Take half to one teaspoon at a time, on its own or in lukewarm water.
products.store: Close tightly and keep in a cool place. Refrigerate after opening to keep it fresh longer.

products.name: Kombu Honey
products.tagline: From single combs hanging on wild branches.

gallery.caption: A dwarf honey bee comb on its branch
A dwarf honey bee comb hanging in dry scrubland
Tiny dwarf bees on their single comb

products.about: Kombu honey is a wild honey made by the dwarf honey bee, the smallest honey bee in India. These bees build a single palm-sized comb that hangs from a thin branch (kombu) in bushes and small trees. Each comb holds only a little honey, so it is collected from the wild in very small quantities. It has a rich, distinct wildflower taste.

A traditional favourite in Tamil homes
products.use: Take a spoonful on its own, or mix with warm water in the morning.

products.tagline: Honey from the blue hills of the Western Ghats.

gallery.caption: A honey bee visiting kurinji flowers

products.about: Neela Kurinji honey comes from the hills of the Western Ghats, where the Neelakurinji shrub turns whole slopes blue when it flowers. The shrub blooms together only about once every twelve years, so honey from these hills is rare and comes in very small batches. It has a delicate, floral taste that is best enjoyed simply.

products.use: Enjoy it straight from the spoon to taste it at its best, or drizzle a little over fruit or curd. Keep it away from heat so the delicate flavour stays.
products.store: Store at room temperature with the lid closed. Always use a dry spoon.
products.bloomNote: Blooms together only about once every twelve years
